themes.name: Proper scoring & elicitation
themes.blurb: What should a verifier be paid for its report? Proper scores for probabilities, intervals, quantiles, rankings and vectors, and the regret each one leaves.

projects.title: Property elicitation for verifiable ML training
projects.summary: Quantile, expectile and Bregman scoring rules, a check that variance is not elicitable alone but is jointly, and a study of pricing benign-drift thresholds for replica verification.

projects.title: How many bits does a probability report need?
projects.summary: Regret of reporting from a finite grid under Brier and log scores: a high-resolution law for the optimal grid (matched to 0.3%), a ln N loss for uniform grids under log score, and a 13× penalty for raw minifloat formats versus symmetrised ones. Stylised.

projects.title: What do risk-averse verifiers report under proper scoring?
projects.summary: Proper scoring rules are truthful only for risk-neutral agents. For a CARA verifier the log score yields reported odds exactly equal to true odds^(1/(1+k)), k = αb; the Brier score yields logit p = logit r + k(2r−1), which the principal can invert exactly. Summing reported logits under-extremises (log-loss 0.332 vs 0.214 at k=2); correcting with the mean k under heterogeneous verifiers is worse than not correcting; a log-score report needs true belief 0.964 to clear a 0.9 accept threshold at k=0.5. A binarised lottery rule is truthful for every increasing utility at a 2.6–27% certainty-equivalent cost. Stylised.

projects.title: What does a verifier's silence tell you?
projects.summary: When reporting costs c, a truthful verifier paid the score gain over an anchor α abstains exactly when |p−α| < √c (Brier) or KL(p‖α) < c (log), so silence is an interval of signals and carries evidence unless the anchor is a symmetric prior. At prior 0.1 the outcome rate among reporters is 0.57; an aggregator that drops silent verifiers has log-loss 0.62 against 0.02 for one that uses silence at n=12 (it worsens as verifiers are added); a stale anchor makes silence point at the wrong state. Quadrature and seeded Monte Carlo. Stylised.

projects.title: How do you price the tail of benign drift?
projects.summary: A drift tolerance is a quantile, but compensation depends on expected shortfall, which is not elicitable alone (a mixture moves ES 1.6→2.24). The scale-free score ln e + (v + (x−v)<sub>+</sub>/(1−α))/e − 1 elicits (VaR, ES) jointly with exact excess law; misreporting ES by a factor r costs ln r + 1/r − 1 (0.307 at ½, 0.193 at 2), matched to quadrature within 2·10<sup>−5</sup>. A quantile-only tolerance leaves ES/VaR = a/(a−1) uncovered under Pareto drift (6× at a=1.2); auditing needs ~2,000 samples for a 20% understatement at index 4 and the CLT plan fails for index ≤ 2. Stylised.

projects.title: Should you pay verifiers for their calibration?
projects.summary: A verifier reporting expit(aL+b) for the true posterior logit L is overpaid-for-error by exactly E[(r−p)²] under Brier and E[KL(p‖r)] under log score. Brier is bounded (a hard 0/1 report still beats the prior at μ=1) but log is not: raw log score ranks a higher-resolution verifier first only for slope a in (0.264, 2.49), so at a=4 a weaker calibrated verifier wins, while recalibrated scores never reverse. Recalibrating on n outcomes costs about tr(HI<sup>−1</sup>)/2n excess Brier (0.264/n, simulation within ~10% for n≥100), beating raw pay beyond n≈20–80. Quadrature and seeded simulation. Stylised.

projects.title: Should a verifier's continuous drift report be scored by CRPS or log score?
projects.summary: For Gaussian reports N(m,s²) both rules have exact expected scores. Overconfidence costs at most σ(√2−1)/√π = 0.234σ under CRPS but is unbounded under log (4995 nats at s=0.01σ); mean errors cost linearly versus quadratically; CRPS is 1-Lipschitz in the realised outcome (log slope 75/σ in our example); a plug-in fit from n samples costs 5σ/(8√πn) versus 1/n; and per-round score variance is finite for Student-t tails ν>2 (CRPS) versus ν>4 (log), which matters for sequential tests. Gaussian family, one verifier. Stylised.

projects.title: Can a verifier be paid for reporting drift variance?
projects.summary: Not from one re-execution (variance’s level sets are not convex), but two independent ones suffice: D=(y<sub>1</sub>−y<sub>2</sub>)²/2 is unbiased with variance σ<sup>4</sup>(κ+1)/2. Brier excess is exactly (r−σ²)²; the scale-free loss D/r+ln r has excess 1/λ+ln λ−1, so halving the report costs 0.307 and doubling 0.193. Catching a 10% misreport at 95% takes about 2–4 thousand tasks (2z²(κ+1)/(λ−1)², simulated 0.93–0.97); disjoint pairs are 1.8× worse than the sample variance at n=10; with Pareto tail index 3 the error decays like m<sup>−1/3</sup>, not m<sup>−1/2</sup>. Stylised.

projects.title: Can the log score be made payable?
projects.summary: Log score is ideal for rare faults but a confident wrong report costs unbounded stake. Extending the log generator past [ε,1−ε] by its second-order Taylor polynomial gives a strictly proper score, identical to log up to a constant inside, with worst-case payment exactly ln((1−ε)/ε)+1/(1−ε). Per unit of payment range it has 63× Brier’s curvature at p=10<sup>−3</sup> but loses to Brier above a closed-form crossover (≈0.07), and ε=p is the best cutoff for truth p.

projects.title: Which proper score should verifiers face with K outcomes?
projects.summary: For K-ary reports the Brier, spherical and log scores have exact regrets and exact worst cases (1−2p<sub>min</sub>+‖p‖² for Brier, ‖p‖−p<sub>min</sub> for spherical). Per unit of payment range the spherical score gives exactly √K times Brier’s incentive at a uniform truth, but both bounded scores nearly ignore a dropped rare class: at a 1% class the loss is 1.3×10<sup>−4</sup> (Brier) and 1.0×10<sup>−4</sup> (spherical) against 0.15 for log. Multiclass follow-up to tangent-log.

projects.title: Can the multiclass log score be made payable?
projects.summary: Extending x ln x below a cutoff ε by its second-order Taylor polynomial gives a strictly proper K-class score that equals −ln r<sub>y</sub> whenever every r<sub>j</sub>≥ε and has payment range exactly 1−ln ε, the same for any K. Per unit of range it has 3× Brier’s rare-class incentive at a 5% class and 63× at 0.1%, the best cutoff is the rarest class’s mass, and a verifier that zeroes out a 1% class loses a closed-form 0.005 (Brier 1.3×10<sup>−4</sup>, log unbounded). Closes the gap left open in categorical-scores.

projects.title: What does it cost to pay for a ranking instead of probabilities?
projects.summary: A verifier who reports only the order of K classes can be paid with a score linear in the outcome indicator. It is strictly proper, and swapping two classes at adjacent ranks costs exactly (p<sub>i</sub>−p<sub>j</sub>)(w<sub>r</sub>−w<sub>r+1</sub>), linear in the gap. Per unit of payment range that beats a Brier-derived ranking whenever the gap is below 1/(K−1) (2.5× at gap 0.1, 250× at 0.001, K=5). Equal spacing maximises the smallest incentive, ranking everything costs K−1 times the mode, a top-k set costs the same as the mode, and the sample size to detect a swap is identical to Brier’s.

projects.title: Should severity reports be scored with the order in mind?
projects.summary: For ordered fault severities the ranked probability score is Brier on the cumulative distribution: strictly proper with exact regret Σ(R<sub>k</sub>−P<sub>k</sub>)², so moving mass ε a distance d costs exactly dε² where Brier charges 2ε² for every d. Pooling adjacent classes costs exactly half of Brier’s, and every threshold probability is within √regret of the truth. The price: per unit of payment range RPS gives Brier’s incentive only for a maximal-distance shift (1/(K−1) for adjacent ones). Extends categorical-scores.

projects.title: Can we elicit the mode of a mixture of honest and cheating drift?
projects.summary: When some workers cheat, drift is a mixture and the mean, which squared loss elicits, lands where almost no task lies (at a 30% cheater 6σ away, the mean’s window holds 0.15 of the mass versus 0.48 at the mode). The mode is not elicitable, but the centre of the width-2α window with the most mass is, with the bounded loss 1[|y−r|>α]. Regret is an exact window-mass difference; the best window is α=σ for normal drift and γ/√3 for Cauchy (no mean exists); an equal bimodal mixture has one α-mode iff α exceeds a closed-form root α*; and under 10–40% contamination the sample α-mode has ~0 bias while the mean is off by 5ε, at a 3.7× RMSE cost when clean.

projects.title: Can a verifier be paid for a tolerance interval, not a point?
projects.summary: The Winkler interval score is strictly proper for the pair of quantiles, with closed-form regret and an optimal expected score of exactly 4sφ(z)/α. Misreporting the width by the same factor costs more when narrow at 95% coverage but more when wide at 80%, so there is no universal rule that overconfidence is worse. Under Cauchy drift the scores have no mean, yet paired differences are bounded, so evaluate verifiers against a benchmark report.

projects.title: How should a tolerance interval be paid for?
projects.summary: The Winkler interval score is the sum of two pinball losses: proper for the equal-tailed quantile interval with exact regret (2/α)[PR(l,α/2)+PR(u,1−α/2)], finite even for Cauchy drift where the expected score does not exist, but its payment grows without bound in the miss distance. A width-plus-miss loss (u−l)+λ1[miss] is bounded by width+λ and elicits the density level set, the shortest interval for its coverage: 22–31% narrower than equal-tailed on lognormal(0,1) drift. The price is statistical: to detect a 20% understatement of a normal tolerance it needs 3–48× more tasks for α≥0.1 and about the same at α=0.01.

projects.title: How should a verifier's vector report be scored?
projects.summary: For a report of an expected drift r ∈ ℝd with noise covariance Σ, every quadratic Bregman score −(y−r)TA(y−r) is proper and charges a misreport D exactly DTAD. Against a trusted reference the per-task gap has exact mean DTAD and variance 4DTAΣAD for any noise law, and Cauchy–Schwarz shows A=Σ−1 has the best signal to noise for every deviation at once, needing 4z²/(DTΣ−1D) tasks. An isotropic score has efficiency at least 4κ/(1+κ)² (Kantorovich), attained by a deviation split between the extreme eigendirections: 25× more tasks at condition number 100, and power 0.29 against 0.80 at 48 tasks in simulation. Per-layer normalisation alone barely helps; with Σ estimated from m reference draws, efficiency is 0.61 at m=2d and 0.95 at m=100. Quadratic scores, trusted reference, finite covariance.

projects.title: What does a verifier's score gap cost in decisions?
projects.summary: Exact calibration functions turning a proper-score gap into a certified cap on accept/audit/slash regret: Brier transfers as ε², log as a KL, polyhedral hinge linearly but without proper elicitation, and an audit action tightens the guarantee; the certificate is never violated in simulation and is attained by a two-point verifier. Stylised.

projects.title: Which surrogate should train a verifier that can escalate?
projects.summary: Reject-option surrogates for accept/reject/escalate decisions: the generalised-hinge conditional risk embeds the Bayes action at its kinks, regret transfers linearly with constant exactly 2d (grid-verified), logistic transfer degrades as 2d(1−d)/δ, and a negative result shows logistic-plus-thresholds still learns faster in scalar SGD. Stylised.

projects.title: How do you pay a verifier whose report decides the job?
projects.summary: If a report of “fault” gets the job rejected and the outcome is seen only on acceptance, scoring observed jobs is improper: verifiers shade under the threshold to get scored, and every job is accepted (1.1–2.8× optimal decision loss at thresholds 0.7–0.2). A reserve payment for rejection makes truth optimal iff the score’s entropy minimum τ<sub>s</sub> is at least the threshold τ<sub>d</sub>, and then it is unique, 1+τ<sub>d</sub>²−2τ<sub>d</sub>τ<sub>s</sub>. Plain Brier (τ<sub>s</sub>=½) therefore fails above τ<sub>d</sub>=½; recentring the score by a term linear in the outcome fixes every threshold, cheapest at τ<sub>s</sub>=τ<sub>d</sub> with rent τ<sup>3</sup>/3. Exploration with inverse-propensity payment is also proper but multiplies payment variance by about 1/ε. Stylised, single verifier.

projects.title: What if the referee itself is noisy?
projects.summary: When verifiers are paid against a judge whose label flips with rates e<sub>0</sub>, e<sub>1</sub>, any proper score elicits the noisy probability e<sub>0</sub>+γp (γ=1−e<sub>0</sub>−e<sub>1</sub>), the Brier incentive shrinks by γ², and rankings of truthful verifiers reverse at η*=0.25. The backward-corrected surrogate score is exactly unbiased for the true loss, at a 1/γ payment spread and (balanced case) 1/γ² more evidence; misestimated rates produce a closed-form affine bias whose cost falls as 1/m in gold checks. Stylised.

projects.title: Can audits be predictable without corrupting scores?
projects.summary: If truth arrives only on audited tasks and the audit rate depends on the report (say g(r)=a+br), “score when audited” is no longer proper: the verifier shades by about −bp(1−p)/(2(a+bp)) and, for steep b, hides at r=0 (Brier excess 0.25 at p=0.5). Weighting the audited loss by 1/g(r) is exactly proper for any audit rule, at variance E[B²]/g−L² and payout cap 1/g<sub>min</sub>; the Neyman audit allocation minimises variance but gains only 3–11% over uniform. Stylised.

projects.title: Can a calibration test certify a verifier?
projects.summary: No. A hedger with no information at all keeps its expected calibration error below √(K+1)(1/(2K)+1/√T) against any outcome sequence, even one that sees its forecast distribution: ECE 0.016 at T=2000 while its Brier score is 0.254 against 0 for a verifier who knows the rule. A lazy constant forecaster is slashed; the hedger passes every calibration threshold tried, but a Brier-gap test against an informed benchmark catches it in 100/100 runs.

projects.title: Can a protocol pay workers to report how often honest replicas agree?
projects.summary: Yes, from two runs and no more: the squared error against the agreement indicator is proper for the collision probability Γ=Σpi2 with exact regret (r−Γ)2, and one run provably cannot (the level sets are not convex). The all-pairs U-statistic has exact variance and needs about a quarter of the runs of disjoint pairs (variance ratio 0.27 at n=100). A fleet of H equal hardware classes has Γ=1/H, so strict equality over k honest replicas false-slashes with probability 1−H1−k. Colluders returning one common wrong value leave agreement unchanged at ε=2Γ/(1+Γ), so Γ cannot be used alone. Runs are i.i.d. and float32 fleets are simulated summation orders.

themes.name: Effort & peer prediction
themes.blurb: Paying for costly checking when effort is hidden and ground truth may never arrive.

projects.title: Peer-prediction markets for decentralized ML training verification
projects.summary: Proper scoring rules, Peer Truth Serum, Correlated Agreement and LMSR aggregation, with eight follow-ups on mechanism-aware adversaries (trust farming, whitewashing, closed-loop attackers) and defences. Pure-Python, dependency-free.

projects.title: What does it cost to pay a verifier to check?
projects.summary: Effort elicitation with proper scoring rules in an exact beta-binomial model: implementable efforts are the concave envelope of the value curve, Brier information rent is exactly (n−1)/(a+b) times effort cost, and the log score needs half Brier's payout spread on rare-fault priors. Stylised.

projects.title: What does a proper score buy when effort is private?
projects.summary: Scoring-rule payments as moral-hazard contracts for costly inference: a closed-form shirking threshold (matched to 1%), first-best effort at scale equal to marginal value with a fee, and under limited liability only 48–65% of first-best surplus, with log score cheaper than Brier at high effort. Stylised.

projects.title: How do you pay for effort when nobody knows the truth?
projects.summary: Peer prediction for unverifiable labelling and judging work: output agreement pays 1.0 for always answering the majority label versus 0.68 for honesty, the Dasgupta–Ghosh payoff is exactly 2p(1−p)g<sub>i</sub>g<sub>j</sub>, effort becomes a coordination game with a closed-form threshold (12.8× higher for rare-positive tasks), and a cost-optimal gold-check rate √(c·g<sub>H</sub>/G) removes the shirking equilibrium. Stylised.

projects.title: Does agreement pay reward shared laziness?
projects.summary: Multi-task peer prediction pays 2G·Cov of two reports. If lazy verifiers copy a shared per-task default (the same public model’s guess) pay becomes 2G[a<sub>i</sub>a<sub>j</sub>pq + (1−a<sub>i</sub>)(1−a<sub>j</sub>)d(1−d)], effort is a coordination game with threshold a* = (k/2G + s)/(pq + s), and the all-lazy profile is always an equilibrium paying 2G·d(1−d): equal to honest pay when the default matches the prior, 1.19× it at p=0.3, d=0.5. Closing it with gold checks needs payment mass (2Gs+k)/(1−acc<sub>D</sub>), larger than the honest pay itself. Stylised.

projects.title: How noisy is peer-prediction pay with finitely many tasks?
projects.summary: The plug-in multi-task payment (agreement minus the agreement implied by empirical frequencies) is exactly twice the sample covariance of two verifiers’ reports, so its variance is available in closed form and matches full enumeration; it is √2 less noisy than drawing fresh penalty tasks and pays a constant reporter exactly 0. Under limited liability a verifier who does no work still collects a noise rent ≈ σ/√(2π) (0.020 against 0.208 honest at n=100). A deductible removes it in closed form, but killing 99% of the rent costs the honest verifier 54% of its pay. Detection needs 56–329 tasks for g=0.7–0.3 (simulated power 0.94–0.95), and ranking two close verifiers takes ~870. Binary conditionally independent reports. Stylised.

projects.title: When most verifiers miss a fault, who should be believed?
projects.summary: If a fault is flagged by fewer than half of the verifiers (0.45 detection, 0.05 false alarms), majority vote is wrong on faulty jobs with probability 0.84 at n=101 and 0.96 at n=301. The surprisingly-popular rule (verdict plus predicted verdict fraction) reduces for truthful Bayesian verifiers to an exact fraction threshold θ = v/(1−u+v) and errs 2.1×10−5 on faulty jobs at n=101, needing 47 votes for 10−3 total error against 36 for a Bayes rule that knows the detector. A wrong believed prior wrecks finite-n accuracy (0.51 error), a wrong believed detector quality breaks the limit, and Byzantines who vote clean and predict “everyone flags” break it at exactly 13.6%. Stylised, truthful reports assumed.

projects.title: Why should the first verifiers be sealed?
projects.summary: Verifiers who are paid for being right and see earlier verdicts herd: once two more revealed signals point one way than the other, everyone copies. With signal accuracy a the cascade is wrong with probability exactly (1−a)²/(a²+(1−a)²) (0.155 at a=0.7) and forms after 2/(a²+(1−a)²) revealed signals (3.4), so accuracy is capped at 0.845 however many verifiers join, versus ≈1 for an independent majority of 101. A sealed first batch of m ≥ 3 lifts the cap (0.875 at m=3, 0.949 at 11) and beats a majority of the same paid size. Recursion checked against fully Bayesian simulated agents. Stylised, symmetric signals.

projects.title: When should a paid verifier stop checking?
projects.summary: A verifier who checks a claim one noisy check at a time and stops when it likes, paid a proper score, follows a symmetric threshold rule (confirmed against dynamic programming over all policies). Accuracy is pk = 1/(1+((1−a)/a)k) and expected checks are k(2pk−1)/(2a−1), exactly. Participation needs a score scale κ ≥ 4c/(2a−1)² under Brier (log needs about half), Brier’s threshold is ln(κ(2a−1)²/((1−a)c))/λ within one step, and adaptive stopping matches a fixed-sample verifier’s accuracy with 2–3× fewer checks. Binary state, known accuracy.

themes.name: Verification games & slashing
themes.blurb: Stake, audits, bribes and disputes: the equilibrium economics of refereed and optimistic verification.

projects.title: Economics of refereed verification
projects.summary: Inspection-game equilibrium for optimistic verification: stake substitutes for re-execution, extra verifiers dilute rewards (free-riding saturates), and joint tolerance/stake design under floating-point drift. Stylised model.

projects.title: Bribing the verifiers
projects.summary: Closed-form bribe floor for buying verifier silence in refereed verification: a sharp collusion-proof stake (falls as 1/m verifiers), and planted-fault jackpots that lift the floor. Verified against brute force and Monte Carlo. Stylised model.

projects.title: Do verifiers and solvers learn the audit equilibrium?
projects.summary: Hedge dynamics in the inspection game: a conserved potential, a closed-form cycle period (matched to simulation within 0.1%), time-averages that converge while per-round audit probability collapses, and optimistic Hedge that converges last-iterate. Stylised.

projects.title: Many verifiers, one solver: the volunteer's dilemma in refereed verification
projects.summary: Closed-form m-verifier audit equilibrium (detection pinned at s/(s+S), redundancy bounded by ln(1/(1-q))/q, cheating rising with m under split rewards), a saddle-point stability result, Hedge dynamics that concentrate audit burden on a subset, and bandit learners that need an exploration floor. Stylised.

projects.title: Are stake and audits substitutes in trace verification?
projects.summary: Sampled audits of a committed training trace under capped slashing: cheating payoff is convex in the number of corrupted steps, and deterrence holds iff min(F, f·k) ≥ T·g. Stake and audits are complements, so stake must scale with job length. Exact hypergeometric computation. Stylised.

projects.title: What does secret task assignment buy?
projects.summary: Random k-fold replication with slashing against a colluding fraction β of workers: with secret assignment cheating is a coordination game and honesty is the unique equilibrium iff S ≥ Gβ<sup>k−1</sup>/(1−β<sup>k−1</sup>), geometric in k; with public assignment colluders cheat only on all-friend jobs, so corruption is β<sup>k</sup> at any stake; a leak probability λ leaves a λβ<sup>k</sup> floor, so each order of magnitude of leakage costs about two replicas. Formulas match Monte Carlo. Stylised.

projects.title: How should a scarce audit budget be spread?
projects.summary: Refereed verification with jobs of different gain and harm: a best-responding cheater is deterred iff the audit probability reaches g/(g+S), so allocation is a knapsack (deter a set exactly, spend the rest on one job). Density greedy with a partial-only candidate has a proved 1/3 guarantee and is within 1% of optimal on 91% of random instances; uniform auditing needs up to 1.9× the budget to deter everything and still leaves 26% of harm at that budget; gain heterogeneity lowers deterrence cost (Jensen); stake substitutes for audits via Σ g/(g+S) = B. Stylised.

projects.title: How many verifiers does deterrence-by-audit need?
projects.summary: Stake sets the audit rate a = G/(G+S); the audits then form a queue with offered load R = λas. Erlang-C waiting matches simulation (P(wait) 0.409 vs 0.407), and square-root staffing c = R + 1.06√R is within 1.5 servers of the exact minimum for R ≥ 100, so the spare capacity needed falls from 60% at R=5 to 1.1% at 104. Stake and headcount trade off with first-order optimum G+S = √(ws G/(rd0)): total cost 23.6 at the optimum versus 76.8 with too little stake and 65 with too much. Heavy-tailed audit times make Allen–Cunneen pessimistic (0.97 vs 0.63); batches of simultaneous audits make it optimistic (0.82 vs 1.45 at batch size 4). Stylised costs, FIFO, static outages.

projects.title: Escalating bonds: cheap challenges, fixed deterrence, a γ-fold capital asymmetry
projects.summary: Bond-escalation dispute games with a fallible oracle, solved exactly: the opening bond that deters false challenges is εV/((1−ε)C−εD) and shrinks geometrically in rounds (20.4 to 10<sup>−5</sup>) while the attacker's total outlay barely moves (20.41 to 20.62); against a capital-limited attacker the honest defender needs exactly γ·max{C(r)≤B<sub>C</sub>} ≤ γB<sub>C</sub>, so the responder pays γ per exchange. Stylised.

projects.title: How wide should a dispute bisect?
projects.summary: Arity and leaf size of k-ary bisection dispute games for refereed verification: the optimal arity solves k ln k − k + 1 = a/b (binary only if a/b ≤ 2ln2−1), arity 10 is 1.9× cheaper than binary at a million steps and 6× at a/b=1000, exact adaptive schedules gain at most about 1%, early-stopping with referee re-execution saves 9–56%, and latency just widens arity. Verified on an executable SHA-256 dispute. Stylised.

projects.title: Can stake shorten a challenge window when proposers can be bribed?
projects.summary: In optimistic verification a fraud pays G unless a challenge is included within w blocks; the attacker controls each proposer w.p. ρ and otherwise pays b to censor. The exact attacker recursion V(n) = ρV(n−1) + (1−ρ)max(−S, V(n−1)−b) gives a closed-form deterrence window (0 mismatches in 5000 instances; Monte Carlo agrees) with a gamble-first, bribe-last optimal attack. A luck-only analysis underestimates the window 100–170×; with an exogenous bribe price the window is 63 blocks for every stake from 10 to 1600; if the bounty is paid as a priority fee the price becomes θS and S·w ≈ G/((1−ρ)θ). Stylised.

Code and white paper

Can a verifier be paid for a tolerance interval, not a point?

The Winkler interval score is strictly proper for the pair of quantiles, with closed-form regret and an optimal expected score of exactly 4sφ(z)/α. Should drift tolerances be per layer or on the total?

Giving each of L layers its own tolerance lets a prover hide the sum of them: L·c(L,α)σ versus zα√Lσ for one test on the total, 6.6× more at L=16 and 23× at L=128. The sum test’s power depends only on the total shift; the exact (Šidák) max test’s depends on how it is spread, the prover’s best split is even (log Φ is concave), and the max test catches a 2.7σ one-layer shift half the time but lets 16σ through spread over all 16 layers. Code and white paper

How do you pay a verifier whose report decides the job?

If a report of “fault” gets the job rejected and the outcome is seen only on acceptance, scoring observed jobs is improper: verifiers shade under the threshold to get scored, and every job is accepted (1.1–2.8× optimal decision loss at thresholds 0.7–0.2). A reserve payment for rejection makes truth optimal iff the score’s entropy minimum τs is at least the threshold τd, and then it is unique, 1+τd²−2τdτs. Plain Brier (τs=½) therefore fails above τd=½; recentring the score by a term linear in the outcome fixes every threshold, cheapest at τs=τd with rent τ3/3. Exploration with inverse-propensity payment is also proper but multiplies payment variance by about 1/ε. Stylised, single verifier. Pure-Python, 10 tests.

Code and white paper

How should a tolerance interval be paid for?

The Winkler interval score is the sum of two pinball losses: proper for the equal-tailed quantile interval with exact regret (2/α)[PR(l,α/2)+PR(u,1−α/2)], finite even for Cauchy drift where the expected score does not exist, but its payment grows without bound in the miss distance. A width-plus-miss loss (u−l)+λ1[miss] is bounded by width+λ and elicits the density level set, the shortest interval for its coverage: 22–31% narrower than equal-tailed on lognormal(0,1) drift. The price is statistical: to detect a 20% understatement of a normal tolerance it needs 3–48× more tasks for α≥0.1 and about the same at α=0.01. Pure-Python, 9 tests.

How well does Freivalds' check work in floating point?

Checking a claimed matrix product by A(Br) ≈ Cr needs a tolerance t, so the error bound becomes size-dependent: a rank-one corruption of Frobenius norm F is missed by a Gaussian probe with probability exactly erf(t/(√2F)), rank one is the worst case for fixed F, and m probes give erfm (4 probes for 1% at 3t). Rademacher probes miss a two-entry corruption with probability ½ at every size. Emulated float32 noise grows ≈n0.9; a hashed probe with free retries lets a cheater grind in 1/erf tries (125 at 100t). Who trades decides how liquid a verification market should be

A wrong b costs log loss only in a transient whose peak is scale-free in m and 1.5–2.4× worse when overconfident; the LMSR subsidy tends to b* ln 2, exactly the spread the GM maker charges. How many honest runs does a slashing tolerance need?

Pure-Python, 7 tests.

Code and white paper

What does a fee do to a prediction market’s price?

A proportional fee f on an LMSR verification market gives every trader an exact no-trade band [q/(1+f), (q+f)/(1+f)] of width f/(1+f), so an informed trader leaves the price at q/(1+f). At price ½ a signal of log-likelihood ratio λ moves the price iff f < tanh(λ/2) = 2a−1, above which the market is dead; fee revenue on a monotone path is exactly fb ln((1−p0)/(1−pT)). Code and white paper

How big should a random verifier committee be?

Drawing m verifiers from a pool of N with B Byzantine, majority capture is exactly hypergeometric: zero once m ≥ 2B+1 and up to 26× below the with-replacement binomial (N=100, B=30, m=41: 1.4×10−4 vs 3.6×10−3). For failure 2−40 the exact size is a steady ≈0.90 of ln(1/ε)/KL(½‖β) while Hoeffding over-sizes it up to 2.2×. With stake-weighted draws only the Byzantine stake share counts: 20 of 100 nodes at 4× stake capture a 41-member committee half the time. A threshold-t rule trades wrong acceptance (2.7×10−7 to 1.1×10−16) against stalls (2.7×10−7 to 3.3×10−2). Static adversary, exact computation. Pure-Python, 11 tests.

Code and white paper

Can a calibration test certify a verifier?

No. A hedger with no information at all keeps its expected calibration error below √(K+1)(1/(2K)+1/√T) against any outcome sequence, even one that sees its forecast distribution: ECE 0.016 at T=2000 while its Brier score is 0.254 against 0 for a verifier who knows the rule. A lazy constant forecaster is slashed; the hedger passes every calibration threshold tried, but a Brier-gap test against an informed benchmark catches it in 100/100 runs.

Code and white paper

When should a paid verifier stop checking?

A verifier who checks a claim one noisy check at a time and stops when it likes, paid a proper score, follows a symmetric threshold rule (confirmed against dynamic programming over all policies). Accuracy is pk = 1/(1+((1−a)/a)k) and expected checks are k(2pk−1)/(2a−1), exactly. Participation needs a score scale κ ≥ 4c/(2a−1)² under Brier (log needs about half), Brier’s threshold is ln(κ(2a−1)²/((1−a)c))/λ within one step, and adaptive stopping matches a fixed-sample verifier’s accuracy with 2–3× fewer checks. Code and white paper

Why should the first verifiers be sealed?

Verifiers who are paid for being right and see earlier verdicts herd: once two more revealed signals point one way than the other, everyone copies. With signal accuracy a the cascade is wrong with probability exactly (1−a)²/(a²+(1−a)²) (0.155 at a=0.7) and forms after 2/(a²+(1−a)²) revealed signals (3.4), so accuracy is capped at 0.845 however many verifiers join, versus ≈1 for an independent majority of 101. A sealed first batch of m ≥ 3 lifts the cap (0.875 at m=3, 0.949 at 11) and beats a majority of the same paid size. Recursion checked against fully Bayesian simulated agents. Code and white paper

How many verifiers does deterrence-by-audit need?

Stake sets the audit rate a = G/(G+S); the audits then form a queue with offered load R = λas. Erlang-C waiting matches simulation (P(wait) 0.409 vs 0.407), and square-root staffing c = R + 1.06√R is within 1.5 servers of the exact minimum for R ≥ 100, so the spare capacity needed falls from 60% at R=5 to 1.1% at 104. Pure-Python, 8 tests.

Code and white paper

When most verifiers miss a fault, who should be believed?

If a fault is flagged by fewer than half of the verifiers (0.45 detection, 0.05 false alarms), majority vote is wrong on faulty jobs with probability 0.84 at n=101 and 0.96 at n=301. The surprisingly-popular rule (verdict plus predicted verdict fraction) reduces for truthful Bayesian verifiers to an exact fraction threshold θ = v/(1−u+v) and errs 2.1×10−5 on faulty jobs at n=101, needing 47 votes for 10−3 total error against 36 for a Bayes rule that knows the detector. A wrong believed prior wrecks finite-n accuracy (0.51 error), a wrong believed detector quality breaks the limit, and Byzantines who vote clean and predict “everyone flags” break it at exactly 13.6%. Stylised, truthful reports assumed. Pure-Python, 7 tests.

Code and white paper

What is a seat in a prediction market worth?

In a sequential LMSR verification market the verifier in position k earns in expectation b·I(y; sk | s<k), a conditional mutual information, so seat rents telescope to the maker’s expected loss (at most b ln 2); an explicit cost-function simulation agrees to three decimals. Rents fall with position, the successive ratio approaching e−C (Chernoff information) from below; order only redistributes a fixed total (a 0.9-accurate verifier gets 0.368 of 0.407 first, 0.303 last). With entry cost c, accuracy improves roughly as 1/b: 11 verifiers at b=0.25 (92%), 41 at b=5 (99.6%). Myopic traders, symmetric signals, monotonicity numerical. Pure-Python, 8 tests.

Code and white paper

How should a model be cut across devices of unequal speed?

For a fixed pipeline order, greedy filling is an exact test of a target stage time (agreeing with an independent dynamic program, with and without memory caps), and every order satisfies W/V ≤ T* < W/V + m wmax/V. A speed-blind equal split costs exactly v̄/vmin times the lower bound (2.40× at log-speed spread 0.5, 8.25× at 1.0) while speed-aware cutting stays within 1.4% at 240 layers. What is left is the device order: at 14 layers and 6 devices the worst order is 1.34× the best, fast-first and slow-first sorts do no better than an arbitrary order (all about 1.16× optimal), and pairwise-swap search gets within 1.1%; the penalty fades to 1.03× at 224 layers. Memory that shrinks as speed grows inflates the bottleneck 1.7×. No communication cost, static speeds. Pure-Python, 8 tests.

Code and white paper

What does it cost to skip the slowest workers?

Waiting for the fastest k of n workers has exact round time s + (Hn−Hn−k)/μ for exponential tails, and for Pareto tails the mean is finite iff n−k+1 > 1/α, so with α ≤ 1 waiting for everyone has infinite expected round time. For SGD on a quadratic the time to accuracy has a minimum k and an interior optimum (34× faster than waiting for all at zero fixed cost, 1.12× at large fixed cost). If speed correlates with data, the fastest-k average is biased by Σ(πi/k−1/n)θi; Horvitz–Thompson reweighting removes it but only pays when the bias is large.

Code and white paper

Does a bigger swarm learn more from shared rollouts?

Not without incentives. With diminishing returns and a peer-rollout discount θ, symmetric Nash play gives every agent exactly the learning level of a lone agent whatever the swarm size (total effort caps at (a/c−1)/θ), while the efficient level grows linearly in N: welfare per agent is 4.5× higher at N=256. At θ=1 a single agent generates everything. A Pigouvian matching subsidy covering θ(N−1)/(1+θ(N−1)) of cost implements the optimum exactly, and junk rollouts beat honesty iff c−ε > p(τ+F).

Code and white paper

What does it cost to make workers race?

If a round pays the first k of n finishers a prize R and workers buy speed at cost c per unit rate, the win probability’s slope at the symmetric point telescopes to (1−k/n)(Hn−Hn−k), so equilibrium speed is R(n−k)(Hn−Hn−k)/(nc) and the round time is exactly nc/((n−k)R). Paying every finisher buys no speed at all; for a fixed budget, speed alone wants winner-take-all (0.10 at k=1 versus 3.2 at k=16 for n=32), and only the statistical floor on k justifies more winners. Recruiting more workers barely helps: total speed bought saturates at kR/c. Exponential races, linear cost, symmetric risk-neutral workers; equilibrium checked on a grid. Pure-Python, 12 tests.

Code and white paper

Who drops out of a race when workers have unequal costs?

If only the first k of n finishers are paid, a slow worker entering at a vanishing rate wins with probability rate × E X(k) of the fast workers, which gives an exact exit rule: workers with cost ratio cs/cf ≥ nf/(nf−k) stay out entirely, and paying k ≥ nf never excludes anyone (checked by best-entry payoffs at thresholds 4/3, 2, 4). At cost ratio 4 with four fast workers, k ≤ 3 shuts the slow ones out and k=4..7 readmits them (share of prizes 0.21→0.46 against a fair 0.5). The note also proves the telescoping identity behind the symmetric race and shows that with convex speed cost, headcount does buy speed. Two cost types, exponential races, grid-checked equilibria.

Code and white paper

How should a router treat modules that are usually asleep?

If only awake modules report and each awake module’s wealth is multiplied by 1+η(ℓ̂−ℓi), the ledger is exactly budget balanced, sleeping wealth never moves (each regime keeps a private ledger), and a module’s regret against the market on its awake rounds is at most ln(1/πi)/η + ηni in its own awake time (the exponential variant pays ηT/8 and is not budget balanced). Admitting a module with wealth ε costs each incumbent ln(1/(1−ε))/η in its bound. With recurring regimes the ledger matches the per-round oracle (0.1004 vs 0.1000, regret about 2.7 whatever the number of specialists) while a forced-to-report Hedge sits at the generalist (0.30) and fixed share is worse (0.34–0.36). The bound is loose (measured regret 2.7 against a bound near 103); losses bounded, wake sets exogenous. Pure-Python, 8 tests.

Code and white paper

How stale can a shared rollout be before it is worthless?

With Gaussian policies whose mean has moved by δ standard deviations, the importance weight has exact moments E w = 1 and E w² = eδ², so the effective-sample fraction is e−δ² (0.37 at δ=1) and a learner needing fraction ρ accepts a lag of √ln(1/ρ)/drift policy versions. Truncating weights has closed-form lost mass, bias and variance (matched by simulation); the best cap cuts the mean-shift estimator’s MSE 1.9× at δ=1, 12.8× at δ=2 and about 750× at δ=3, and finite-sample ESS is optimistic once weights are heavy-tailed. Equal-variance Gaussians, one statistic. Pure-Python, 7 tests.

Code and white paper

How should a verifier's vector report be scored?

For a report of an expected drift r ∈ ℝd with noise covariance Σ, every quadratic Bregman score −(y−r)TA(y−r) is proper and charges a misreport D exactly DTAD. Against a trusted reference the per-task gap has exact mean DTAD and variance 4DTAΣAD for any noise law, and Cauchy–Schwarz shows A=Σ−1 has the best signal to noise for every deviation at once, needing 4z²/(DTΣ−1D) tasks. An isotropic score has efficiency at least 4κ/(1+κ)² (Kantorovich), attained by a deviation split between the extreme eigendirections: 25× more tasks at condition number 100, and power 0.29 against 0.80 at 48 tasks in simulation. Per-layer normalisation alone barely helps; with Σ estimated from m reference draws, efficiency is 0.61 at m=2d and 0.95 at m=100. Quadratic scores, trusted reference, finite covariance. Pure-Python, 7 tests.

Code and white paper

Can a module game a ledger by choosing when to sleep?

Yes, if it declares after seeing its loss. The wealth ledger pays each awake module exactly its leave-one-out saving, ηWA(1−pi)Si, but a module that sleeps whenever its own loss exceeds θ earns ηpBθ(1−θ)/2 per unit wealth against an equal-skill honest rival (best 1/8 at θ=1/2) and takes the market from a 0.1 share in about 130 rounds, while the router’s realised loss stays at 0.5. Declared before the router serves, the same wealth is a real saving that falls from 0.125 to 0.011 as the module’s signal about its own loss gets noisier. A sleeping tax that stops the exploit must be at least ηpB/2, a fixed-share rate that halves an honest specialist asleep 90% of the time in 6 rounds, so commitment, not taxation, is the fix. Two modules, uniform losses, threshold strategies; mean-field predictions 3–8% slow. Pure-Python, 9 tests.

How should a router pick k distinct experts?

Sparse mixture-of-experts routing as a capped Hedge market: expert prices are min(1, λ wi) with a single shadow price λ and an exact KL projection. Regret against the best fixed k-set stayed within k ln(N/k)/η + ηTk/2 in every run (41–58% of it, not proved here); plain normalisation prices an expert above 1 in 282 of 300 rounds and understates loss 3.2×; systematic sampling realises exactly k distinct experts with 8–14× lower loss variance. Oblivious losses only. Pure-Python, 6 tests.

Code and white paper

How many skipped training steps hide in the loss noise?

If a worker paid for T steps runs only (1−f)T, the verifier’s log-loss test (null sd σ′, level α) hides exactly the compute at which the loss curve, inverted, crosses the noise band: L((1−f*)T) = L(T)eσ′(zα+zP). For a power law with a loss floor this is closed form and grows as the reducible share r falls (6% at r=1 but 64% at r=0.05 for σ′=0.02). On exactly solvable quadratic GD the predicted detection probability matches simulation within 1.5 points, and the loss test is worth only about 4.4 random step audits at best (0.16 once training is floor-dominated). Stylised: one statistic, normal approximation, known curve family. Pure-Python, 14 tests.

Code and white paper

How much does an appeal ladder of juries buy, and what must appeals cost?

A dispute goes to 3 jurors; the loser may pay a fee (proportional to panel size) to appeal to 11, then 27. If the fee lies in the window V(1−q) ≤ j n < V q, only the wrongly ruled truthful side appeals and the final error is exactly the product of the tiers’ error rates; below the window both sides appeal and only the last tier counts, above it nobody appeals. With jurors 70% accurate and prize 100 the smallest deterring panel is 11 (23 at prize 1000, 41 at 104); the 3→11→27 ladder errs 2.4×10−4 at 5.8 expected juror seats, against 12.6% for a single 7-seat panel, while a 9-juror middle tier leaks 0.78 wrong-side appeals per dispute. If jurors share a common bias with probability ρ, error cannot fall below ρ(1−a) however many tiers are added. Independent jurors, myopic appeals, no juror incentives or bribery; exact results agree with 200,000-trial simulation.

projects.summary: Under Brier loss the best verifier is the one whose report is closest to the outcome frequency q, and each pair has an anytime-valid betting e-process growing at KL(q‖midpoint). Certifying the leader means beating every rival, so the delay is ln(1/α) over the smallest such rate, which belongs to the rival whose midpoint with the leader is nearest q: the best rival on the opposite side of q, not the runner-up (rate 0.0026 against 0.0086 in a six-verifier league). A bet mixture certifies within 1.35–1.60× of the oracle prediction; successive elimination cuts verifier evaluations 4cuts evaluation cost 2–4× at n=8–12ndash;5× at n=8–12; a peeking z-test declares a false strict best in 59% of exact-tie runs against 1.6% for the e-process. Stylised: fixed reports, i.i.d. tasks.

projects.title: How much can Byzantine verifiers move an aggregate?
projects.summary: Mean, median and trimmed-mean aggregation of verifier reports under a Byzantine fraction β: mean bias βB is unbounded, median bias σΦ<sup>−1</sup>(1/(2(1−β))) is independent of B and diverges at β=½, trimmed-mean closed form for τ≥β matches simulation, and trimming below β fails. Stylised.

projects.title: Can a verifier tell from old-task losses that a continual-learning job skipped or shortchanged tasks?
projects.summary: Extends the forgetting law to a trainer that skips each task with probability s or takes a step fraction a: the final-checkpoint loss on the task at position t is exactly ρt−1[(1−2m1+m2)(r/d)λk + (r/d)ρ(ρk−λk)], matching exact quadrature and simulation. A skipped task is at least d/(d−r) times worse than a trained one at every lag but clearly so only in a window (ratio ≥2 for lags ≤6.7 at d=16, r=2). Catching a skipping trainer is lag-free: about 17–20 jobs for 20% skipping at any audit lag, scaling as 0.7/s2 and falling with job length, while a 10% step shortfall needs about 9,600 jobs. Stylised: linear regression, Haar-random tasks, known initial error.

themes.name: Markets as routers
themes.blurb: Cost-function and wagering markets as online learners that route among modular, continually learning experts.

projects.title: Markets as routers: LMSR = Hedge, quadratic potential = sparsemax
projects.summary: Cost-function markets as online learners for modular, continual-learning expert routing: verified equivalence and loss/regret bounds, and a switching-environment simulation where the quadratic market stays sparse and low-regret at liquidity levels where LMSR degrades. Small-scale; limitations stated.

projects.title: Wagering mechanisms as routers for modular, continually learning experts
projects.summary: Weighted-score wagering (Lambert et al.) as a budget-balanced, replayable mixture-of-experts gate under recurring regime drift: plain wagering locks in, fixed-share wealth tax repairs it but subsidises free-riders.

projects.title: How much should a router extremize?
projects.summary: Pooling calibrated experts with shared training data: the Bayes-optimal logit exponent a* = n/(1+(n−1)ρ) (matched to a numerical argmin), extra experts saturating at 1/ρ effective experts, naive independence pooling doing worse than chance at ρ=0.9, and an online learner that finds a*. Stylised.

projects.title: What does late feedback cost a market router?
projects.summary: Hedge/LMSR routing of modular experts when losses arrive after device-dependent delays: regret ≤ ln N/η + ηT/8 + ηD/2 with D the total outstanding rounds, so mean delay d̄ inflates the horizon by 1+4d̄; ignoring delay costs 12× regret against a reactive adversary at delay 100, the worst-case tuned rate is too cautious on oblivious data, an observable-count adaptive rate recovers most of it, and LMSR subsidy grows about 20× at mean delay 5. Stylised.

projects.title: Is load balancing a congestion price?
projects.summary: Capacity-constrained expert routing is a softmax with a per-expert price, the Lagrange multiplier of its capacity, and the dual is smooth and concave. Any price vector gives a computable upper bound and, after repair toward the uniform assignment, a feasible lower bound, so a verifier certifies near-optimality from prices alone (gap below 10<sup>−4</sup> at the optimum, always above the true suboptimality). Sign-update balancing has a sampling floor of about 2.5/√B in max relative overload that no step size removes, plus a step-proportional limit cycle on a fixed batch (22.6% at γ=0.2, 1.2% at 0.01). Two-expert Gaussian price of balance is closed form with price shift equal to the median gap; a Hoeffding audit of ln(2N/δ)/(2ε<sup>2</sup>) tokens covered 400 of 400 trials. Synthetic scores only. Stylised.

projects.title: Is risk tolerance the learning rate of a wealth market?
projects.summary: When agents bet a fraction λ of wealth Kelly-style, the clearing price is the λ·wealth-weighted mean belief, total wealth is conserved, and λ=1 is exactly the Bayes mixture. Market log-loss exceeds expert i’s by at most ln(1/s<sub>i</sub>)/λ<sub>i</sub> on any sequence (loose on i.i.d. data), the growth-optimal fraction is (π−p)/(q−p), and moving the price against calibrated others costs Vχ²(p<sub>0</sub>‖p): equal to LMSR b·KL at b=2V for small shifts but 7.5× stiffer at p=0.99. On a truth that switches regimes, full Kelly is wrong about half of every segment (regret about 1630 at T=4000) while λ of 0.1–0.2 cuts it 3–7×. Binary events, static experts. Stylised.

projects.title: How should a router pick k distinct experts?
projects.summary: Sparse mixture-of-experts routing as a capped Hedge market: expert prices are min(1, λ wi) with a single shadow price λ and an exact KL projection. Regret against the best fixed k-set stayed within k ln(N/k)/η + ηTk/2 in every run (41–58% of it, not proved here); plain normalisation prices an expert above 1 in 282 of 300 rounds and understates loss 3.2×; systematic sampling realises exactly k distinct experts with 8–14× lower loss variance. Oblivious losses only.

projects.title: How should a router treat modules that are usually asleep?
projects.summary: If only awake modules report and each awake module’s wealth is multiplied by 1+η(ℓ̂−ℓi), the ledger is exactly budget balanced, sleeping wealth never moves (each regime keeps a private ledger), and a module’s regret against the market on its awake rounds is at most ln(1/πi)/η + ηni in its own awake time (the exponential variant pays ηT/8 and is not budget balanced). Admitting a module with wealth ε costs each incumbent ln(1/(1−ε))/η in its bound. With recurring regimes the ledger matches the per-round oracle (0.1004 vs 0.1000, regret about 2.7 whatever the number of specialists) while a forced-to-report Hedge sits at the generalist (0.30) and fixed share is worse (0.34–0.36). The bound is loose (measured regret 2.7 against a bound near 103); losses bounded, wake sets exogenous.

projects.title: Can a module game a ledger by choosing when to sleep?
projects.summary: Yes, if it declares after seeing its loss. The wealth ledger pays each awake module exactly its leave-one-out saving, ηWA(1−pi)Si, but a module that sleeps whenever its own loss exceeds θ earns ηpBθ(1−θ)/2 per unit wealth against an equal-skill honest rival (best 1/8 at θ=1/2) and takes the market from a 0.1 share in about 130 rounds, while the router’s realised loss stays at 0.5. Declared before the router serves, the same wealth is a real saving that falls from 0.125 to 0.011 as the module’s signal about its own loss gets noisier. A sleeping tax that stops the exploit must be at least ηpB/2, a fixed-share rate that halves an honest specialist asleep 90% of the time in 6 rounds, so commitment, not taxation, is the fix. Two modules, uniform losses, threshold strategies; mean-field predictions 3–8% slow.

themes.name: Prediction-market design
themes.blurb: Liquidity, fees, privacy and manipulation in the LMSR markets that aggregate verifier beliefs.

projects.title: What does not knowing the horizon cost a market maker?
projects.summary: An LMSR with liquidity b routes like Hedge with rate 1/b, but the tuned b needs the horizon T. A b<sub>t</sub> = c√t schedule with c* = 1/(2√ln N) pays exactly √2 over the horizon-aware bound (1.36 rising to 1.41 measured); the doubling trick is 1.70× worse than the continuous schedule against a price-reactive adversary; and self-tuning liquidity b<sub>t</sub> = Δ<sub>t−1</sub>/ln N makes the subsidy equal the accumulated mixability gap (1.3 against 102 on easy data) with regret at most 2Δ. Regret analysis only. Stylised.

projects.title: The subsidy cost of privacy in prediction markets
projects.summary: Differentially private LMSR via the binary-tree mechanism: error scales as 1/(bε), tree noise beats per-release noise ~15×, and privacy noise is exploitable so market-maker loss far exceeds b ln 2. Stylised.

projects.title: Who pays for the information in a manipulated market?
projects.summary: An uninformed manipulator pushing an LMSR verification market from q to τ loses exactly b·KL(q‖τ), which equals to the digit the extra rent it hands to informed traders; the accuracy change is μ[e<sub>1</sub>(1−q) − e<sub>0</sub>q − (1−2q)], positive only in a liquidity band (0.107, 0.413 in the baseline): below it nobody enters and manipulation costs 1−2q accuracy, above b = Nc/(H(q)−ln(1/(1−ε))) entry is certain and manipulation is neutral. Matches an executable LMSR Monte Carlo. Stylised.

projects.title: What does a slippage limit give away in a prediction market?
projects.summary: A searcher who buys before and sells after a victim's LMSR trade extracts exactly the victim's slippage tolerance times its fair cost (εC<sub>0</sub>, error 1.4×10<sup>−14</sup> over 216 instances), with a closed-form front-run of about εb/(1−p) shares, so return on capital falls as 1/b. A proportional fee of about v(1−p)/(2b) makes it unprofitable at any tolerance; the victim's optimal tolerance grows only like √log of the stakes; pro-rata batching keeps 0.989–0.999 of the extraction and uniformly random ordering cuts it exactly 3×. Stylised.

projects.title: Who trades decides how liquid a verification market should be
projects.summary: A Glosten–Milgrom market maker facing an informed share μ with accuracy q moves its posterior log-odds by exactly 2·atanh(μ(2q−1)) per net buy, so its price path is an LMSR with b* = 1/(2 atanh m) (verified to 2×10<sup>−16</sup>). A wrong b costs log loss only in a transient whose peak is scale-free in m and 1.5–2.4× worse when overconfident; the LMSR subsidy tends to b* ln 2, exactly the spread the GM maker charges. Stylised.

projects.title: What does a fee do to a prediction market’s price?
projects.summary: A proportional fee f on an LMSR verification market gives every trader an exact no-trade band [q/(1+f), (q+f)/(1+f)] of width f/(1+f), so an informed trader leaves the price at q/(1+f). At price ½ a signal of log-likelihood ratio λ moves the price iff f < tanh(λ/2) = 2a−1, above which the market is dead; fee revenue on a monotone path is exactly fb ln((1−p0)/(1−pT)). With ten 0.65-accurate traders, the break-even fee (≈0.11) raises Brier error from 0.115 to about 0.16 and revenue is hump-shaped in f. Naive traders, synthetic signals.

projects.title: What is a seat in a prediction market worth?
projects.summary: In a sequential LMSR verification market the verifier in position k earns in expectation b·I(y; sk | s<k), a conditional mutual information, so seat rents telescope to the maker’s expected loss (at most b ln 2); an explicit cost-function simulation agrees to three decimals. Rents fall with position, the successive ratio approaching e−C (Chernoff information) from below; order only redistributes a fixed total (a 0.9-accurate verifier gets 0.368 of 0.407 first, 0.303 last). With entry cost c, accuracy improves roughly as 1/b: 11 verifiers at b=0.25 (92%), 41 at b=5 (99.6%). Myopic traders, symmetric signals, monotonicity numerical.

projects.title: How fast does a prediction market converge when traders only understand part of it?
projects.summary: Traders who each move prices within a subspace of securities make a cost-function market a randomized subspace descent. The market maker’s expected loss telescopes to ½(e0′Ae0 − eT′AeT) whoever trades, so accuracy is bought once. Correlated securities slow single-security traders in closed form (5 securities: 31 rounds to reach 10−3 of the error uncorrelated, 356 at correlation 0.95), while offering A-conjugate bundles restores the exact rate 1−1/d at any correlation. With noisy beliefs the fraction κ a trader moves acts as an SGD step size: floor dκσ2/(2−κ), and a per-security running-mean step beats the best constant step (error 0.26 vs 0.47 at 100 rounds; full steps stay at 5). A simulated 4-outcome LMSR matches the local rate predictions to within 0.01 for two of three bundle designs and is faster than predicted for the third, for a reason not isolated. Quadratic-cost theory with i.i.d. trader arrival and Gaussian belief noise.

themes.name: Paying contributors
themes.blurb: Buying compute, data and model improvements: holdout markets, Shapley payments, contests and races.

projects.title: Paying for improvements, not for overfitting
projects.summary: A model-improvement market paying holdout-loss decreases: the budget telescopes, but naive payment feedback lets a data-less adversary be paid while the published model's true loss worsens; a Ladder-style threshold removes the attack at a measured cost to honest small contributors. Stylised.

projects.title: What does submitting copies earn under Shapley payments?
projects.summary: Paying contributors of data or gradients by Shapley value rewards replication even when copies add zero information: in a Bayesian mean-estimation game the replicator's payment rises with every copy to its stand-alone value, exactly (n+2)/2 times the honest payment against n unit-precision others (5.5× at n=9). If the evaluator treats copies as independent the replicator's pot share tends to 100%; leave-one-out pays true copies exactly zero but distributes only 1/(n+1) of the pot; collapsing duplicates fixes it but underpays independent look-alikes by 45%. Exact computation checked against permutation brute force. Stylised.

projects.title: How should Shapley payments be sampled and audited?
projects.summary: In a saturating contribution game v(S)=1−exp(−Σw<sub>i</sub>) every estimator variance is exact. Permutation sampling always pays out exactly v(N) but is noisy; size-stratified sampling has 6–8× lower variance (exactly zero for equal contributors) yet misses the pot by up to 7% in a run; reversing each permutation cuts RMSE 1.6× at no cost; Hoeffding sample counts are 4–5× larger than needed, and stratification finds the top-3 payees with about 4× fewer samples. Stylised, n≤10.

projects.title: How precise should a training-contest leaderboard be?
projects.summary: In a winner-take-all contest ranked on a noisy holdout of m samples, equilibrium effort is V·a<sub>n</sub>√m/s with a<sub>2</sub>=a<sub>3</sub>=1/(2√π) exactly, but the formula stops being an equilibrium once V/σ² passes a ceiling (12.35, 7.78, 6.11, 5.60, 5.80 for n=2, 3, 5, 10, 20) that sits below the zero-rent limit and falls to half of it at n=20. The organiser's optimal holdout is min(m<sub>cap</sub>, (wVa<sub>n</sub>/2sκ)²): when evaluation is cheap the ceiling, not cost, binds. Quadrature checked against Monte Carlo and brute-force best replies. Stylised.

projects.title: What does it cost to buy decentralised compute?
projects.summary: Reverse auction for k compute units from n devices with private costs: the truthful threshold auction pays exactly k(k+1)/(n+1), twice the winners’ true cost for every n and k (also with a reserve), the buyer-optimal reserve is exactly v/2 (worth up to +1.03 utility in thin markets, nothing once v≥2), and the pay-as-bid equilibrium has closed form and matches revenue (1.3334 vs 1.3333). Stylised.

projects.title: What does it cost to make workers race?
projects.summary: If a round pays the first k of n finishers a prize R and workers buy speed at cost c per unit rate, the win probability’s slope at the symmetric point telescopes to (1−k/n)(Hn−Hn−k), so equilibrium speed is R(n−k)(Hn−Hn−k)/(nc) and the round time is exactly nc/((n−k)R). Paying every finisher buys no speed at all; for a fixed budget, speed alone wants winner-take-all (0.10 at k=1 versus 3.2 at k=16 for n=32), and only the statistical floor on k justifies more winners. Recruiting more workers barely helps: total speed bought saturates at kR/c. Exponential races, linear cost, symmetric risk-neutral workers; equilibrium checked on a grid.

projects.title: Who drops out of a race when workers have unequal costs?
projects.summary: If only the first k of n finishers are paid, a slow worker entering at a vanishing rate wins with probability rate × E X(k) of the fast workers, which gives an exact exit rule: workers with cost ratio cs/cf ≥ nf/(nf−k) stay out entirely, and paying k ≥ nf never excludes anyone (checked by best-entry payoffs at thresholds 4/3, 2, 4). At cost ratio 4 with four fast workers, k ≤ 3 shuts the slow ones out and k=4..7 readmits them (share of prizes 0.21→0.46 against a fair 0.5). The note also proves the telescoping identity behind the symmetric race and shows that with convex speed cost, headcount does buy speed. Two cost types, exponential races, grid-checked equilibria.

themes.name: Decentralised training systems
themes.blurb: Gossip, local SGD, pipelines, checkpoints and shared rollouts on unreliable, heterogeneous workers.

projects.title: What can one stubborn node do to gossip training?
projects.summary: Pairwise gossip averaging as a stand-in for all-reduce: disagreement contracts by exactly (n−2)/(2(n−1)) ≈ ½ per matching round (about 20 rounds at any n), the noise floor is (n−1)(n−2)s²/n (matched to 0.3%), a single stubborn node captures the honest mean at exact rate 1−1/(n(n−1)), and a trust-region clip turns capture into linear creep of at most τ/(n(n−1)) per step. Stylised.

projects.title: What does infrequent averaging do to the answer?
projects.summary: Local-SGD / DiLoCo-style averaging of heterogeneous quadratic workers has a closed-form fixed point: a weighted mean of the workers' optima with weights 1−(1−ηa<sub>i</sub>)<sup>H</sup> that saturate, so it is exactly unbiased at H=1, forgets curvature as H grows (converging to the unweighted mean), and is non-monotone in between. Weighting by a<sub>i</sub>/w<sub>i</sub> removes the bias exactly; if the server trusts claimed step counts, a low-curvature worker moves the fixed point from 0.50 to 0.91 by claiming 100 steps instead of 5, tying communication savings to verified work. Wall-clock-optimal H under a bias tolerance is 5.7× faster than H=1 at moderate comm cost, with a non-interval feasible set. Noise formulas match Monte Carlo. Stylised.

projects.title: How often should preemptible workers checkpoint?
projects.summary: Exact checkpoint interval under Poisson churn: w* = (1+W<sub>0</sub>(−e<sup>−1−λC</sup>))/λ, independent of restart cost, with Young/Daly overshooting by 5–25%; intervals within 2× cost under 3.5%; a synchronous job on n workers restarts at rate nλ so efficiency falls to 50% near n≈700, and admitting flaky workers cut throughput five-fold. Stylised.

projects.title: Should a pipeline replicate stages or skip them?
projects.summary: A microbatch crosses L stages held by workers that come and go. The drop probability is the exact binomial tail P(Bin(L,q)>s) with stage outage q = ρ + (1−ρ)(1−a)<sup>r</sup>, so replicas cannot lift success above the shared-domain floor (1−ρ)<sup>L</sup>: at L=48, ρ=10<sup>−3</sup> no r reaches a 1% drop rate, but allowing one skipped stage makes r=3 enough. At a=0.9 a four-stage skip budget cuts the workers for a 10<sup>−3</sup> drop rate from 240 to 96; under a per-skip quality loss κ the cost-optimal design is skip-heavy for cheap skips and moves to replication as κ grows (gain over no-skip 2.9× down to 1.08×). Independent outages, multiplicative skip penalty. Stylised.

projects.title: How should a model be cut across devices of unequal speed?
projects.summary: For a fixed pipeline order, greedy filling is an exact test of a target stage time (agreeing with an independent dynamic program, with and without memory caps), and every order satisfies W/V ≤ T* < W/V + m wmax/V. A speed-blind equal split costs exactly v̄/vmin times the lower bound (2.40× at log-speed spread 0.5, 8.25× at 1.0) while speed-aware cutting stays within 1.4% at 240 layers. What is left is the device order: at 14 layers and 6 devices the worst order is 1.34× the best, fast-first and slow-first sorts do no better than an arbitrary order (all about 1.16× optimal), and pairwise-swap search gets within 1.1%; the penalty fades to 1.03× at 224 layers. Memory that shrinks as speed grows inflates the bottleneck 1.7×. No communication cost, static speeds.

projects.title: What does it cost to skip the slowest workers?
projects.summary: Waiting for the fastest k of n workers has exact round time s + (Hn−Hn−k)/μ for exponential tails, and for Pareto tails the mean is finite iff n−k+1 > 1/α, so with α ≤ 1 waiting for everyone has infinite expected round time. For SGD on a quadratic the time to accuracy has a minimum k and an interior optimum (34× faster than waiting for all at zero fixed cost, 1.12× at large fixed cost). If speed correlates with data, the fastest-k average is biased by Σ(πi/k−1/n)θi; Horvitz–Thompson reweighting removes it but only pays when the bias is large.

projects.title: Does a bigger swarm learn more from shared rollouts?
projects.summary: Not without incentives. With diminishing returns and a peer-rollout discount θ, symmetric Nash play gives every agent exactly the learning level of a lone agent whatever the swarm size (total effort caps at (a/c−1)/θ), while the efficient level grows linearly in N: welfare per agent is 4.5× higher at N=256. At θ=1 a single agent generates everything. A Pigouvian matching subsidy covering θ(N−1)/(1+θ(N−1)) of cost implements the optimum exactly, and junk rollouts beat honesty iff c−ε > p(τ+F).

projects.title: How stale can a shared rollout be before it is worthless?
projects.summary: With Gaussian policies whose mean has moved by δ standard deviations, the importance weight has exact moments E w = 1 and E w² = eδ², so the effective-sample fraction is e−δ² (0.37 at δ=1) and a learner needing fraction ρ accepts a lag of √ln(1/ρ)/drift policy versions. Truncating weights has closed-form lost mass, bias and variance (matched by simulation); the best cap cuts the mean-shift estimator’s MSE 1.9× at δ=1, 12.8× at δ=2 and about 750× at δ=3, and finite-sample ESS is optimistic once weights are heavy-tailed. Equal-variance Gaussians, one statistic.

projects.title: How fast does a shared model forget a task, and does splitting it into modules help?
projects.summary: Training to convergence on random rank-r tasks in Rd is a projection, and the expected loss on a task learned k tasks ago is exactly (r/d)(1−r/d)(ρk−λk): zero when learned, a peak (0.044 at d=12, r=3, lag 2.5) at a lag near 0.7d/r, then decay because the tasks agree; matched by simulation to the third decimal. Routing tasks to m modules dilutes both rates by m and cuts short-horizon forgetting (5.9× at T=4, m=8) but a single shared model minimises seen-plus-fresh loss at every horizon tried, and two modules forget more than one at T=12. With conflicting tasks forgetting has a floor 2rτ²/d that only task-specific modules remove. Stylised: linear regression, exact convergence, isotropic tasks.

projects.title: How should independently trained modules be merged, and how much does parallel training buy?
projects.summary: Averaging m modules trained to convergence on random rank-r tasks has an exact residual error 1−2amp+a2(mp+m(m−1)p2) with p=r/d, needing only isotropy. The optimal scale is 1/(1+(m−1)p) and leaves (1−p)/(1+(m−1)p): plain averaging stalls at (1−p)2 (0.78 vs 0.47 at m=8, d/r=8) and unscaled task arithmetic diverges (56 at m=64). The decay is harmonic, not geometric, so m parallel workers give a wall-clock speedup that grows only logarithmically (8.9× at m=16, 17× at m=64) and halves in efficiency near m≈d/r×2.5. Seen and fresh losses are closed forms matched by simulation. Stylised: linear regression, exact convergence, consistent isotropic tasks.

projects.title: When should a continual learner replay an old task, and does a fixed schedule beat random replay?
projects.summary: Replaying a task alongside each fresh one is a joint projection, so the expected loss on a tracked task is an exact product of 2×2 matrices for any schedule (matched to simulation at every step; recovers the no-replay law). One replay is best at the forgetting-peak lag — 5 at d=32, r=4; 89 at d=128, r=1 — yet removes only 25–42% of total forgetting (replaying at step 1 barely helps at small r/d). A period longer than the peak lag never touches the peak, and a fixed period beats random replay at the same rate only below roughly 1.2–3 peak lags (e.g. 1/8 at d=32, r=4, but random wins at 1/12). Halving forgetting needs a rate 0.25 at d=12, r=3 and 0.015 at d=128, r=1; tasks with 2r≥d are fully recovered by one replay. Stylised: realizable linear regression, exact convergence, one tracked task.

projects.title: How much of an old task must a continual learner store, and is it better to replay a little often or a lot rarely?
projects.summary: If only m of an old task’s r examples are stored, replaying them with a fresh task is “project out the stored subspace, then take a plain step in dimension d−m”. That gives an exact 2×2 mean-state matrix interpolating no replay (m=0) and full replay (m=r, matched to replay-law to 12 digits), agreeing with simulation at every step. One replay at its best step recovers a fraction of the full saving that is nearly linear in m/r (0.23, 0.47, 0.72 at ¼, ½, ¾ for d=12, r=4; within 0.004 of m/r at d=128, r=8). At a fixed rate, half the memory buys 57–65% of the saving. At a fixed budget of examples per step, one large replay beats many small ones, but only by 0.1–2 points of total forgetting in wide models and up to 6 in a tight one (d=12, r=4), so buffer size matters more than schedule. Stylised: realizable linear regression, exact convergence, one tracked task.

projects.title: When continual-learning tasks conflict, how much does a task-aware router of modules actually buy?
projects.summary: With cluster-structured conflicts, the long-run loss on an old task is exactly (2r/d)[τw² + τb²(1 − Purity)], where Purity is one minus the router’s expected Gini impurity (matched to simulation within 0.3–2.3% across six routers). Random routing to any number of modules leaves the whole floor; a perfect router onto m modules removes exactly (m−1)/(K−1) of the between-cluster floor, so half needs 5 of 8 clusters’ worth of modules; and a routing error q costs 2q of impurity at first order (10% error returns 36% of the shared-model floor at K=8, 25% returns 59%). Purity is auditable with an unbiased pair-collision estimator. Stylised: realizable linear regression, exact convergence, Gaussian cluster centres, hard routing.

projects.title: How should the outer optimiser and sync interval be set when workers run H local steps per round?
projects.summary: On a quadratic, H inner steps make the outer optimiser see curvatures 1 − (1 − ηa)H, which saturate at 1: the outer condition number shrinks from κ to about κ/H (1000 → 16.1 at H=64). Per-round rates are exact 2×2 spectral radii (matching literal simulation), the tuned heavy-ball outer step puts every mode at exactly √β*, and the best momentum falls from 0.88 at H=1 to 0.01 at H=1024, so a fixed Nesterov 0.7/0.9 needs 4–8× more rounds. With a sync costing C inner steps, the wallclock-optimal interval is H* ≈ C, worth about √C/2 over syncing every step (16× at C=1000), while plain averaging has no interior optimum. Stylised: noiseless quadratic with a shared Hessian.

projects.title: How much gradient noise survives in DiLoCo-style local SGD, and how should the outer step, momentum, worker count and sync interval be set against it?
projects.summary: On a quadratic with M workers, H noisy inner steps and a heavy-ball outer step, the stationary variance per mode is exactly αV(1+β)/((1−β)s(2(1+β)−αs)) with V the averaged inner noise and s = 1 − (1 − ηa)H, matching literal simulation to 0.2%. At α = 1 the floor is independent of H; for small α more local steps shrink it by less than a factor of 2. Momentum costs no extra floor at equal effective step (and lowers it at large steps), workers give near-linear speedup (331× at M = 256, α still below 1), and unlike the noise-free case the best sync interval grows as the noise-floor target falls (H* = 5, 11, 38 at C = 10), up to 41× faster than syncing every step. Stylised: quadratic, Gaussian noise, shared Hessian, fixed α.

projects.title: What happens to local SGD when workers drop in and out?
projects.summary: Each of N workers joins a round with probability p. Averaging the participants has exact stationary variance αVwm/(s(2−αs)) with m = E[1/K | K≥1]; dividing by the expected count instead is stable only for αs < 2/c, c = 1+(1−p)/(Np), and cannot contract faster than 1−1/c per round (0.22 at N=32, p=0.1). At matched speed the fixed normaliser is quieter at small steps by E[K|K≥1]·E[1/K|K≥1] (1.34×), and averaging wins only at fast rates. Reliable workers bias the fixed point (0.467 instead of 1.000 in our example) unless displacements are inverse-propensity weighted. Matched to simulation within 0.5%. Stylised.

projects.title: What does compressing the pseudo-gradient cost local SGD, and is it better than syncing less often?
projects.summary: Unbiased compression of each worker's displacement (rand-k, relative variance ω) gives an exact stationary variance αVw(1+ω)/(N s((2−αs)−αsω/N)) and shrinks the stable outer step to 2/(s(1+ω/N)): more workers restore the step (0.47 → 2.44 for ω=99, N=16 → 256) but never the floor, which stays (1+ω)×. Norm-scaled (QSGD-style) quantisation has a closed form through one scalar T = E|d|2; at equal error energy its loss equals coordinate-wise at H=1 and is about 10% worse at H=16, with the stiff mode's variance doubling. For equal bytes, syncing 1/ρ times less often leaves the floor unchanged at α=1 while keeping a fraction ρ multiplies it by 1/ρ. Matched to simulation within 2%. Stylised: quadratic, shared curvature (no client drift), unbiased compressors only.

projects.title: How much outer step does overlapping communication with compute cost, and how many rounds should be in flight?
projects.summary: Applying the averaged displacement τ rounds late obeys zτ+1 − zτ + c = 0 with c = αs, so the stable step is exactly c < 2 sin(π/(4τ+2)) ≈ π/(2τ+1): 2, 1, 0.62, 0.45 for τ = 0…3, shrinking like 1/τ. The fastest single-mode rate is the double root τ/(τ+1), and the stationary noise floor is an exact Yule–Walker solve (closed form (1+c)/((1−c)c(2+c)) at τ = 1) that matches literal delayed-DiLoCo simulation to 0.3%. Delay is free at small steps (+1% at α = 10−3, τ = 4) but multiplies the floor by 3.9× at c = 0.8. At an equal floor each delay round costs only about 6% more rounds, so the wall-clock-optimal delay is exactly ⌈latency / compute time⌉ (1.9–7.5× faster than no overlap). Stylised: constant delay, identical workers, quadratics, no momentum.

projects.title: Does error feedback rescue the noise floor that compressed local SGD loses?
projects.summary: Workers keep the unsent part of their displacement and add it to the next message. On a quadratic with random sparsification the second moments close exactly: stability requires αs < 2(2−ρ)Nρ/(Nρ2+4(1−ρ)) — half the unbiased limit for a single worker, above the uncompressed limit for large cohorts — and the floor has a closed form that returns to the uncompressed one at small steps (1.08× at ρ=¼ where unbiased compression pays 4×) while the mean keeps its speed. What the residual buys is unbiasedness: dropping converges to the send-rate-weighted mean, feedback to the true mean, but at a variance that only pays off for very small steps. Top-k is simulation only; stylised quadratics.

projects.title: How should a server weight workers that ran different numbers of inner steps?
projects.summary: With worker i running Hi steps, weighted averaging has exact floor α2Σwi2Vi/(r(2−r)), r = αΣwisi. One worker's information is I∞tanh(λH/2): H=8 carries 20% of the ceiling and H=64 93%, so a fast device is worth far less than its step count. Information-optimal weights span at most 2×, hence equal weights lose at most 9/8 (measured ≤1.09), whereas step-proportional (FedAvg-style) weights lose up to 1.76× per mode and 10.5× on three modes when one worker in eight is 256× faster. Matched to simulation within 1%. Stylised: quadratic, shared optimum (no client drift), fixed Hi.

projects.title: What does a median or trimmed-mean outer step cost local SGD, and what does it buy against Byzantine workers?
projects.summary: Because the median and trimmed mean commute with shifts, the outer loop stays exactly linear: floor αVwv/(s(2−αs)) plus a bias Vwm2/s2, with the same stability limit as averaging. With no attackers the median costs N·Var = 1.35 to 1.56 (→ π/2). With a fraction ε of attackers its bias is bounded (Φ(z) = 1/(2(1−ε)): 0.18 noise-sigmas at ε = 1/8) and beats averaging once the attack offset exceeds about 1.4 sigmas; more workers shrink only the variance part (total loss 0.103 → 0.102 from N=8 to 128), while a longer inner loop shrinks the bias (39× from H=1 to 256). Trimming exactly the attacker count is worse than the median. Matched to simulation within 1.3%. Stylised: quadratic, Gaussian noise, shared curvature, constant-offset attackers.

themes.name: Digital twins & sim-to-real
themes.blurb: What a simulated clone of a physical system is worth for training and validating controllers: transfer regret, validation, and randomization.

projects.title: What is a digital twin worth for training a controller?
projects.summary: In a scalar linear-quadratic plant the twin-trained gain has exact deployment regret, asymmetric with a stability cliff: underestimating actuation to 0.21× is infinitely costly while 2× over costs 0.22. A twin can score perfectly on passive logs (log-score gap exactly 0) yet mistrain the controller, and closed-loop logs are blind along Δa = kΔb, so validation needs designed probing. Used as a ridge prior, a twin with bias δ is worth exactly σ2/(vδ2) real probe steps at every accuracy target (22 steps at δ=0.3), and removes small-sample divergence (3.1% to 0 at n=10). Matched to simulation within 1–4%. Stylised.

projects.title: How wide should domain randomization be, and what does it buy?
projects.summary: Randomizing the twin's input gain over ±ε trains a more conservative gain (monotone in ε; small-width law kε−k* = −(εb)2Jkbb/(6Jkk)) at a quartic price when the twin was right, and moves the deployment stability cliff out by about 15%. At 2.3× the twin's gain the nominal controller has regret 84 versus 1.4 at ε=0.9. But uniform-average training is not minimax: its worst-case regret exceeds the nominal gain's for ε ≤ 0.7, and the best width equals the prior's half-width, paying off only when the prior reaches the cliff. Stylised.

projects.title: How fast can a deployed digital twin be caught going stale, and when is it invisible?
projects.summary: An e-process on the twin's closed-loop prediction residuals is valid however often it is checked (2.3% false alarms versus 51.6% for a repeatedly refit χ2 test at nominal 5%). Its detection rate is exactly the twin-transfer score gap, affine in the exploration variance v; a mixture-delay formula matches simulated medians within 10–20% (leading order L/rate is 40–55% too fast). Twins on the line Δa = kΔb are invisible under the deployed policy (rate exactly 0) and detectable at rate Δb2v/2σ2 with dither; most of them cost almost nothing (regret 6·10−4) so dither does not pay, but the one that thinks the actuator is nearly dead (regret 0.23) is worth a v≈0.006 dither that cuts expected cost 12×. Stylised.
